content: Babi guling is Balinese spit-roasted suckling pig, seasoned with a paste of turmeric, coriander, chilli, lemongrass, galangal, and shrimp paste. Served with rice, lawar (spiced vegetable-and-coconut mix), and crackling. Most famous at Ibu Oka in Ubud, Warung Babi Guling Pak Malen in Seminyak, and countless village stalls. Not halal — served openly in Bali because of the Hindu population.

Nasi campur (literally 'mixed rice') is a plate of rice with a small selection of side dishes chosen by the customer — typical items include tempeh, tofu, egg, sambal, sayur (vegetables), chicken, and fish. Each region has its own style: Balinese nasi campur is often served with satay lilit and lawar, while Chinese-Indonesian nasi campur includes char siu and braised pork. A cheap, honest lunch (25–50k IDR).

Martabak comes in two very different forms. Martabak manis (sweet martabak, also called terang bulan) is a thick pancake stuffed with chocolate, cheese, condensed milk, peanuts, or Nutella — the classic Indonesian night snack. Martabak telur (savoury) is a thin dough wrap filled with minced meat, egg, and spring onion, pan-fried and served with pickles and curry sauce. Sold at street carts in every city, especially busy after 7 PM.

Mie goreng is Indonesian fried noodles — yellow egg noodles stir-fried with kecap manis (sweet soy), garlic, shallots, chilli, cabbage, and often chicken, prawn or egg. The instant version (Indomie Mi Goreng) is a cultural phenomenon in its own right and available worldwide. The warung version at 15–25k IDR is a filling, cheap comfort meal.

Gado-gado is Indonesia's warm salad — steamed vegetables (long beans, cabbage, bean sprouts, potato, boiled egg, tofu, tempeh) topped with a spiced peanut sauce and prawn crackers. Naturally vegetarian if you skip the shrimp paste (terasi) in the sauce — ask 'tanpa terasi' for a fully vegan version. Excellent light lunch, especially in Jakarta and West Java.

Nasi Padang is the classic Padang-style presentation from West Sumatra: rice served with 10–15 small dishes brought to your table — rendang, gulai ayam (chicken curry), sambal ijo (green chilli), telur balado (spicy egg), sayur nangka (jackfruit curry) — and you pay only for what you eat. Rumah Makan Padang (Padang restaurants) are everywhere in Indonesia. Very spicy by default; ask for 'tidak pedas' if you want mild.

Ayam bakar is Indonesian grilled chicken — marinated in kecap manis, garlic, tamarind, and turmeric, then finished over charcoal. Sold with rice, sambal, lalapan (raw leaves), and a small dish of soup broth. Regional variants: ayam bakar Taliwang (Lombok, super-spicy chilli glaze), ayam bakar Wong Solo (Central Java, sweeter). 30–50k IDR at a warung.

Bakmi is Indonesian-Chinese egg noodles served either dry (bakmi ayam — with braised chicken, greens, and fried shallots) or in soup (bakmi kuah). Popular chains: Bakmi GM, Bakmi Naga, Bakmi Aloi. Almost always served with a side bowl of clear broth and sambal. A good option when you want something less spicy than most Indonesian food.

Es teler is a classic Indonesian dessert drink — shredded ice, jackfruit, young coconut, avocado, condensed milk, and pandan syrup. Cooling, filling, and cheap (15–25k IDR at a warung). Sister dessert es campur (mixed ice) adds cendol (green rice-flour jelly) and grass jelly. Great after a spicy meal on a hot afternoon.
